chunks: From him, from Ibn Ribāṭ, from Ibn Udhaynah, from Muḥammad ibn Muslim, who said:

At times I would enter upon Abū Jaʿfar عليه السلام after I had prayed al-ẓuhr and al-ʿaṣr, and he would say, “Have you prayed al-ẓuhr?” I would say, “Yes, and al-ʿaṣr as well.” Then he would say, “I have not prayed al-ẓuhr.” So he would rise calmly, without haste, and perform ghusl or wudu (ablution), then pray al-ẓuhr and then pray al-ʿaṣr. And at times I would enter upon him while I had not prayed al-ẓuhr, and he would say, “Have you prayed al-ẓuhr?” I would say, “No.” Then he would say, “I have already prayed al-ẓuhr and al-ʿaṣr.”

It was said to him: There is nothing in these reports that contradicts what we have presented, because his statement عليه السلام, “All of that is broad,” is to be understood as meaning that all of that is permissible, having been allowed by the shari'ah, even if some of it has merit over some other. There is nothing in the report to indicate that all of that breadth is equal in merit. And it is possible that this was permitted for them due to a kind of taqiyyah and consideration of expediency; what he narrated indicates that.

key_terms.وَاسِعٌ: broad in allowance; accommodating within the law
key_terms.ٱلتَّقِيَّةِ: dissimulation for protection in adverse circumstances

ai.seo_question: Does this hadith show flexibility in the timing and order of al-ẓuhr and al-ʿaṣr prayers?
ai.summary: This report discusses the performance and timing of al-ẓuhr and al-ʿaṣr prayers in the presence of Abū Jaʿfar عليه السلام, showing variation in practice. The appended discussion explains that such variation indicates permissibility within the shari'ah, while still allowing that some forms may be more meritorious than others, and it also raises the possibility of taqiyyah.
